readerTitle: Your best tutors will be the first to leave
caseNote: 가상 사례 (온라인 과외 마켓플레이스, 지역 화물 마켓플레이스) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 마켓플레이스를 열 때는 '누구를 먼저 모을까'와 '좋은 매칭이 플랫폼 밖으로 빠져나가지 않을까'를 처음부터 함께 설계해야 한다.
misconception: 좋은 공급자만 모으면 끝이다. 수수료 회피는 연락처 공유를 막으면 해결된다.

sources.text: PIXO BMO-05-02 (Which side to build first), BMO-05-05 (Disintermediation)의 개념을 적용
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 과외 계산: 회당 $50, 수수료 20% = $10, 튜터 수령 $40. 주 1회 × 36주(학기 기준 가정) = 수수료 $360. 직거래 $45 가정 시 학부모 절약 $5 × 36 = $180, 튜터 추가 수입 $5 × 36 = $180. 합계 $360으로 수수료와 일치.
화물 마켓플레이스 수수료 15%, 주 1회 반복 노선 등은 모두 가상 수치입니다. 실제 화물 중개 수수료 수준을 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
과외 시장에서 직거래 이탈이 흔하다는 점은 일반적 관찰로만 서술했고 특정 기업의 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your best tutors will be the first to leave
body: Maya is launching an app that connects parents with math tutors in her city. Parents book and pay in the app. She keeps 20% of each lesson.
She has a small budget and two big problems ahead. One shows up on day one. The other shows up only after things start working.

image.label: A tutor and student at a kitchen table, a phone showing a booking app
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 부엌 식탁에서 튜터와 고등학생이 수학 문제를 풀고, 식탁 위 휴대폰에 예약 앱 화면. 문 밖에서 학부모가 튜터에게 현금 봉투를 건네려는 작은 장면을 배경에 살짝. 실제 앱 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: Where should Maya spend her first month?
body: Parents search hard when exams are close. Good math tutors are scarce and already busy.
With one month and a small budget, what does Maya do first?

options.text: Run ads to parents across the city
options.feedback: Parents will come, find three tutors with no free slots, and not return. Spending on the easier side first wastes the visit.

options.text: Personally recruit 30 strong tutors for high-school exam math in one city
options.feedback: This is **which side to build first**: start with the scarce side, in a narrow slice. Parents who arrive find real choices and open times.

options.text: Launch every subject nationwide so no one finds it empty
options.feedback: Breadth feels safe, but it spreads a few tutors thin across many searches. Each parent still sees almost nobody near them.

cards.title: It worked. Then repeat bookings dropped.
body: Maya signed up 30 tutors. Parents found open slots, and the first 100 lessons were booked in six weeks.
But something odd showed up. Tutors stayed busy, and parents said they were happy. Yet second and third bookings between the same parent and tutor kept falling.
The matches were good. They just weren't happening in the app anymore.

cards.title: Why both sides want to leave.
body: If they meet at $45 in cash, the parent saves **$180** and the tutor earns **$180** more. The fee is a prize they can split.

breakdown.label: Lesson price
breakdown.detail: What the parent pays in the app

cards.callout: Tutoring is weekly, personal and long-running. That makes each match easy to take offline.

cards.title: How should Maya keep the matches?
body: Maya needs repeat lessons to stay in the app. Which approach works best?

options.text: Hide phone numbers and ban tutors caught taking cash
options.feedback: This fights **disintermediation** with rules, but parents and tutors meet in person every week. You lose your best tutors and still can't see the cash.

options.text: Cut the fee on repeat lessons and make the app worth using: easy rescheduling, makeup lessons, progress notes
options.feedback: This makes staying cheaper than leaving. You earn less per lesson but keep the relationship, which is the defense against **disintermediation**.

options.text: Charge a bigger fee for the first match, then let pairs go
options.feedback: A one-time finder's fee accepts **disintermediation** instead of fighting it. It can work, but you give up a year of revenue for one payment.

cards.title: Some leakage is the price of a good match.
body: No design keeps every pair. A long, trusting relationship is exactly what a tutoring app sells, and it is also what makes going direct easy.
So measure it. Track lessons per parent-tutor pair over time, not just new sign-ups. If pairs fade after lesson two, the fee is bigger than the value the app adds to each lesson.

cards.title: Now it's trucks and factories.
body: You run a regional freight marketplace. Small manufacturers post loads, and local trucking firms bid. You take 15%.
One shipper now books the same carrier on the same route every week. What do you do?

options.text: Keep 15% on every load, same as one-off jobs
options.feedback: A repeat route needs no matching. Paying full price for help they don't need invites both sides into **disintermediation**.

options.text: Offer a lower contract rate for regular routes, plus tracking, invoicing and a backup truck if one breaks down
options.feedback: You charge for what still adds value. A backup truck matters to a factory, so staying beats a phone call.

options.text: Focus only on urgent one-off loads and give up regular routes
options.feedback: Urgent loads are where matching is worth most. But you give up steady volume, which is often what keeps carriers on your platform.

cards.softwareNote: The same pattern shows up in freelance and agency platforms: once a client finds a developer they like, ongoing work tends to move to direct contracts unless the platform adds value to every invoice.

cards.title: Get the hard side first, then earn every repeat.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **Which side to build first:** start with the scarce side in a narrow slice. **Disintermediation:** when matches repeat, the fee must buy something each time.
**Try it today:** list where your customers deal with the same partner again and again. For each, write what you still do for them on the tenth deal.
